concepts.name: Profit follows capital
concepts.description: When everyone invests for the same time, profit is shared in the ratio of capitals.

concepts.name: Capital and time together
concepts.description: Different amounts for different periods: share in the ratio of capital × months.

concepts.name: Joining late and changing capital
concepts.description: Break the year into stages and add up capital × months across them.

concepts.name: Working partners
concepts.description: A working partner takes a commission first; the rest is shared by capital and time.

formulas.title: Equal time
formulas.prompt: Partners invest for the same period. How is profit divided?
formulas.explanation: With equal time, each rupee earns the same, so profit is in the ratio of capitals.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A invests ₹6,000 and B ₹4,000 for a year. Profit is ₹5,000. What does A get?

formulas.title: Capital × time
formulas.prompt: Partners invest different amounts for different periods. How is profit divided?
formulas.explanation: A rupee invested for two months earns twice as much as a rupee invested for one, so capital and time both count.
formulas.commonMistake: Using capital alone or time alone.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A puts in ₹4,000 for 12 months and B ₹6,000 for 8 months. In what ratio is profit shared?

formulas.title: Changing capital
formulas.prompt: A partner joins late or changes capital. How do you handle it?
formulas.formula: Capital-months = Σ (capital in each stage × months in that stage)
formulas.explanation: Add the capital-months of every stage, then compare partners.
formulas.commonMistake: Using the final capital for the whole year.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A invests ₹20,000 and withdraws ₹5,000 after 6 months. What are A's capital-months for the year?

formulas.title: Working partner
formulas.prompt: One partner manages the business for a commission. How is the profit split?
formulas.formula:
Commission = c% of the profit (paid first)
Rest shared by capital × time
formulas.explanation: The manager takes the commission off the top, then also shares the remainder as an investor.
formulas.example:
Profit ₹10,000, manager A gets 10% = ₹1,000
Rest ₹9,000 split 2 : 3
formulas.commonMistake: Applying the commission to the manager's share only.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A manages the business for 10% of the profit. Capitals are ₹6,000 and ₹9,000; profit is ₹10,000. What does A get in all?

formulas.title: Equal profits
formulas.prompt: Two partners earn equal profits but invested for different periods. How do their capitals compare?
formulas.formula: Capital ratio = inverse of the time ratio
formulas.explanation: Profit follows capital × time, so equal profits mean the two products are equal.
formulas.example: A invests for 12 months and B for 8 months with equal profits: capitals are in the ratio 8 : 12 = 2 : 3.
formulas.commonMistake: Giving the capitals in the same ratio as the times.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A joins for the full year, B for 9 months, and they share the profit equally.

levels.title: Profit Follows Money and Time
levels.description: How to divide profit fairly when partners put in different amounts for different periods.

blocks.title: Each rupee earns the same
blocks.body: If every rupee earns the same profit each month, a partner's share depends on how many rupee-months they put in. With equal time, it is simply the ratio of capitals.

blocks.title: The share ratio
blocks.caption: Simplify the ratio, then divide the profit into parts.

blocks.title: Joining late
blocks.body: A partner who joins after 3 months is invested for only 9 of the 12 months. Multiply capital by the months actually invested. If the capital changes mid-year, add up each stage.

levels.title: Partnership Formulas
levels.description: Capital, capital × time, stage changes and working partners.

levels.title: Direct Profit Sharing
levels.description: Capital ratios and equal-capital time ratios.

levels.title: Time, Joining and Commission
levels.description: Capital × months, late joiners and managers.

levels.title: Unknown Capitals and Multiple Stages
levels.description: Work back to a capital; multi-stage investments.

questions.question: A invests ₹6,000 and B invests ₹4,000 in a business for one year. The profit is ₹5,000. What is A's share?
questions.explanation: The capitals are in the ratio 6 : 4 = 3 : 2, so A gets 3/5 of the profit: 5,000 × 3/5 = ₹3,000.

hints.text: Simplify the ratio of capitals first.

questions.question: A and B invest in the ratio 3 : 5 for the same period. The profit is ₹16,000. What is B's share, in rupees?
questions.explanation: Total parts = 8, so one part = ₹2,000. B gets 5 parts = ₹10,000.
questions.method: Divide the profit by the sum of the ratio terms.

hints.text: How many equal parts are there in all?

questions.question: A, B and C invest ₹5,000, ₹7,000 and ₹8,000 for a year. The profit is ₹10,000. What is B's share, in rupees?
questions.explanation: Total capital = ₹20,000, so B gets 7/20 of the profit: 10,000 × 7 ÷ 20 = ₹3,500.

hints.text: Add the three capitals to get the total.

questions.question: When partners invest different amounts for different lengths of time, the profit is divided in the ratio of
questions.explanation: A rupee invested for longer earns more, so both the amount and the duration count: capital × time.

hints.text: A rupee left in twice as long should earn twice as much.

questions.question: A and B invest equal amounts. A invests for 12 months and B for 8 months. In what ratio should they share the profit?
questions.explanation: Equal capital, so the ratio of times decides: 12 : 8 = 3 : 2.

questions.question: A invests ₹4,000 for 12 months and B invests ₹6,000 for 8 months. The profit is ₹9,600. What is A's share, in rupees?
questions.explanation: Capital-months: A = 4,000 × 12 = 48,000 and B = 6,000 × 8 = 48,000. They are equal, so the profit splits equally: ₹4,800 each.

hints.text: Multiply each capital by its months.

commonMistakes: Sharing by capital only: 4 : 6 gives A ₹3,840.

questions.question: A starts a business with ₹8,000. After 3 months B joins with ₹12,000. At the end of the year the profit is ₹8,500. What is B's share?
solutionSteps: A invests for 12 months, B for 9.
questions.method: B is in the business for 12 − 3 = 9 months.

hints.text: How many months is B invested?

commonMistakes: Using 12 months for B, which gives A a smaller share than deserved.

questions.question: A starts with ₹20,000 and B with ₹30,000. After 6 months A withdraws ₹5,000. At the end of the year the profit is ₹19,000. What is A's share, in rupees?
questions.method: Add the capital-months of each stage.

hints.text: Split A's year into two stages.

questions.question: A and B invest ₹6,000 and ₹9,000. A also manages the business and receives 10% of the profit as commission before the rest is divided in proportion to capital. The profit is ₹10,000. How much does A receive in all?
questions.explanation: Commission = ₹1,000. The remaining ₹9,000 is split 6 : 9 = 2 : 3, giving A ₹3,600. A's total = 1,000 + 3,600 = ₹4,600.
questions.method: Commission first, then share the rest.

hints.text: A gets two amounts: commission and investor share.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the commission (₹3,600) or the investor share (₹1,000).

questions.question: A invests ₹5,000 for 6 months, B invests ₹4,000 for 9 months and C invests ₹6,000 for 4 months. The profit is ₹7,500. What is C's share, in rupees?
questions.explanation: Capital-months: A 30,000, B 36,000, C 24,000 → ratio 5 : 6 : 4. There are 15 parts, so one part = ₹500 and C gets 4 × 500 = ₹2,000.

hints.text: Multiply each capital by its months, then simplify.

questions.question: A invests ₹15,000 for the whole year. B joins after 4 months. At the end of the year the profit is shared between A and B in the ratio 2 : 1. How much did B invest, in rupees?
questions.explanation: A: 15,000 × 12 = 180,000. B invests for 8 months, so B's capital-months are 8b. The ratio 180,000 : 8b = 2 : 1 gives 8b = 90,000 and b = 11,250.
questions.method: Set up the capital-months ratio and solve for the unknown capital.

hints.text: How many months is B invested?

questions.question: A invests ₹9,000 for the whole year. B invests ₹8,000 for the first 6 months and then adds ₹4,000 more, keeping ₹12,000 in for the last 6 months. The profit is ₹19,000. What is A's share, in rupees?
questions.method: Add capital-months across B's two stages.

hints.text: Split B's year into two stages.

commonMistakes: Using ₹12,000 for the whole year for B.

questions.question: A and B invest in the ratio 3 : 2 for one year. A manages the business and takes 20% of the profit as a salary; the rest is shared according to capital. The total profit is ₹10,000. How much does B get?
questions.method: Salary off the top; B only shares the remainder.

hints.text: Which amount is left to divide by capital?
